title: Classification of Groups of Order pq via Sylow's Theorems
description: A complete Lean 4 proof of the pq-group classification theorem: for distinct primes p < q, every group of order pq is cyclic when p does not divide q-1. The proof uses Sylow's third theorem to show the Sylow q-subgroup is always unique (hence normal), and the Sylow p-subgroup is unique when p ∤ q-1. When both are normal, a commutator argument shows they commute, and the product of generators has order pq.

overview.historicalContext: The classification of groups of order pq for distinct primes p < q was completed by Burnside in 1911 using Sylow's theorems. The result shows: if p does not divide q-1, there is exactly one group of order pq up to isomorphism (the cyclic group ℤ/pq); if p divides q-1, there are exactly two — the cyclic group and a non-abelian semidirect product ℤ/q ⋊ ℤ/p. This is among the most elegant applications of the Sylow theorems and is a standard exercise in abstract algebra courses.
overview.problemStatement:
Let p < q be distinct primes and G a finite group of order pq.

**Main Theorem**: If p does not divide q-1, then G is cyclic (isomorphic to ℤ/pq).

**Converse direction**: If p divides q-1, there exists a non-cyclic group of order pq (the semidirect product ℤ/q ⋊ ℤ/p), and any non-cyclic group of order pq has exactly q Sylow p-subgroups.

**Concrete examples**:
- Order 15 = 3·5: 3 ∤ 4, so only ℤ/15
- Order 21 = 3·7: 3 | 6, so ℤ/21 and a non-abelian group of order 21
- Order 35 = 5·7: 5 ∤ 6, so only ℤ/35
- Order 6 = 2·3: 2 | 2, so ℤ/6 and S₃
overview.proofStrategy:
**Step 1 (Unique Sylow q-subgroup)**: n_q divides p (the index of any Sylow q-subgroup) and n_q ≡ 1 (mod q). Since p < q, if n_q = p then p ≡ 1 (mod q), impossible since p < q. So n_q = 1.

**Step 2 (Sylow p-subgroup analysis)**: n_p divides q (prime) so n_p ∈ {1, q}. If n_p = q then q ≡ 1 (mod p), i.e., p | q-1. Contrapositive: if p ∤ q-1 then n_p = 1.

**Step 3 (Cyclicity from two normal subgroups)**: When both Sylow subgroups P (order p) and Q (order q) are normal:
  - P ∩ Q = {1}: elements in both have order dividing gcd(p,q) = 1
  - Elements of P and Q commute: the commutator g⁻¹k⁻¹gk lies in both P and Q, hence is 1
  - Generators g ∈ P, k ∈ Q have orders p, q and commute, so gk has order pq = |G|
  - G = ⟨gk⟩ is cyclic
keyInsights: The key constraint p < q forces n_q = 1 unconditionally: n_q | p and n_q ≡ 1 (mod q), but n_q ≥ 2 would require n_q ≥ q+1 > p, contradicting n_q | p.
The commutator argument for cyclicity is a general technique: two normal subgroups of coprime order generate their direct product.
The order-of-product formula `Commute.orderOf_mul_eq_mul_orderOf_of_coprime` is the key Mathlib lemma connecting commutativity of generators to the order of their product.
The non-abelian case when p | q-1 is witnessed by the unique non-trivial homomorphism ℤ/p → Aut(ℤ/q) ≅ ℤ/(q-1), which constructs the semidirect product ℤ/q ⋊ ℤ/p.
prerequisites: Cyclic groups and orders of elements
Direct products of groups of coprime order

conclusion.summary: The pq-group classification is fully verified: the uniqueness of the Sylow q-subgroup, the cyclicity criterion, and the concrete examples are all machine-checked with 0 sorries and 0 axioms. The core cyclicity proof from two normal Sylow subgroups is an original 80-line Lean 4 construction.
conclusion.implications: This result is the prototypical example of how Sylow's theorems constrain group structure. The same technique — bounding Sylow numbers to force normality, then using commutator arguments — extends to classify groups of many other orders and underlies large portions of finite group theory.
openQuestions: Can the non-abelian case (when p | q-1, there is exactly one non-abelian group of order pq) be fully formalized, including the uniqueness up to isomorphism?
What is the complete classification of groups of order p²q for primes p, q — can the Sylow methods be systematized into a decision procedure?
